analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 20% for all cardholders.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in May 2008 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to make it illegal for a credit card company to charge an annual percentage rate above 20% on a credit card account. At the time, many card issuers charged rates well above that, especially on borrowers with weaker credit, and there was no national cap on credit card interest rates. The bill was introduced by Rep. Maurice Hinchey with five Democratic cosponsors in May 2008 and was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: People who carry a balance on a credit card. Anyone paying an interest rate above 20% — typically borrowers with lower credit scores whom issuers charge the highest rates — would see their rate capped, lowering the monthly finance charges on existing balances and slowing the pace at which card debt grows. In 2008, with a recession underway and households leaning on credit cards, that would have meant real savings for the households least able to afford double-digit compounding interest.

how_it_helps.text: It writes a national cap into the Truth in Lending Act: no credit card account under an open-end consumer credit plan could carry an annual percentage rate above 20%, no matter the borrower's credit score or the issuer's pricing model.

Because the cap applies to any extension of credit on a card account, it covers the rates charged on existing revolving balances, not just new purchases — so cardholders already paying over 20% would see the direct benefit.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies that profit from card interest. Issuers would no longer be able to price cards above 20%, cutting into the interest income earned on their riskiest, highest-rate accounts. Some issuers responded to rate caps by tightening access to credit or shifting costs to fees, so some marginal borrowers might have found cards harder to get.

drawbacks.text: A 20% cap is a blunt instrument: issuers price risk with interest rates, and a hard ceiling can lead them to deny credit outright to marginal borrowers or recover the difference through higher fees, so some of the people the bill aims to help could lose access to credit instead of getting cheaper credit.

The cap leaves 20% standing — a rate that would still cost a household carrying a $5,000 balance roughly $1,000 a year in interest — and imposes no limits on fees, penalty pricing, or other charges issuers could use in place of rate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to households carrying above-20% balances would have been substantial and immediate, and the bill was simple — one sentence added to existing law, no new bureaucracy. The honest cost is that a hard national rate cap can push some risk-priced borrowers out of the credit card market entirely or onto fee-heavy products, and even under this bill a cardholder could still legally be charged 20%. It was a meaningful but partial fix, and one that Congress ultimately delivered a version of a year later through different means (the 2009 Credit CARD Act addressed rate hikes and penalty pricing without a rate cap).

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2008 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on May 7, 2008, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Reps. McDermott, Grijalva, Lee, Kucinich, and Woolsey.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day it was introduced.
That referral was the last action ever taken on the bill — the committee never reported it out, and no chamber ever voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill proposed adding a single subsection to the Truth in Lending Act prohibiting any credit card annual percentage rate above 20%.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers are better off, because nothing limited the rates they could charge — issuers continued charging rates above 20% to their highest-risk customers for years after the bill died. Cardholders paying those rates got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap credit card interest rates at 20% and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died in committee at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 110th Congress.

against.name: Credit card issuers and the banking industry
against.role: Industry affected by the rate cap
against.what_they_did: Card issuers opposed national interest rate caps, which would cut into interest income on high-rate accounts.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; there was no recorded floor vote to show how the broader chambers would have split.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and consumer finance companies)
industries.note: Issuers earned large shares of card revenue from rates above 20%, charged mostly to weaker-credit borrowers; the cap would have eliminated that pricing tier, cutting their interest income. Their gain from the bill's death is the cost cardholders continued to pay.
